Skills and core rules

9 core rules apply to every change, whether or not a skill loads. The workflow skill then loads only the skills that match the task, from these 24.

Core rules

Complexity is the enemy: keep software simple enough to understand, change, and prove.

  1. Consult sets the engineering bar, and the host owns the mechanics. When they conflict, Consult's bar wins, and the host decides how to meet it.
  2. Keep unrelated parts separate. Make state and effects explicit.
  3. Build only what the user asked for. Build the main behavior first unless safety or data loss requires an edge case now.
  4. Check existing tools before building one. Look for a maintained library before writing code for a solved problem, and prefer mature, proven libraries and tools, on current supported versions, unless the user asks for newer ones.
  5. Write code a reader can follow in one pass. This covers code you write or change; do not reshape untouched code to fit.
  6. Explain the change to the user. Report what needs their attention first, then what changed, why it is better, what proves it, and what remains unproven.
  7. Ask whether backward compatibility is required when a change alters behavior that callers outside the change, or stored data, depend on.
  8. Treat input that crosses a trust boundary as untrusted, even when the request does not mention security.
  9. Static checks count as much as tests. Before you commit or push, run the project's linter and type checker, and its formatter in check mode or on the files you changed.

24 skills

Process and proof

workflow

Loads first for non-trivial code changes to choose skills, sign-off gates, and checks.

proof

Tests and checks that prove acceptance criteria, edge cases, and invariants.

Every acceptance criterion needs a check that fails when the criterion is not met.

code-review

Review diffs and PRs for bugs, regressions, edge cases, and merge readiness.

Findings first. Block on correctness, safety, data loss, and missing proof.

debugging

Reproduce symptoms, isolate causes, inspect evidence, and fix bugs.

No fix without root-cause evidence.

refactoring

Behavior-preserving change, tests, and safe rewrites.

Green before the refactor. Green after each step. Never mix structure and behavior in one commit.

Design

specify

Read the code, propose a design, and agree on it before building: tradeoffs, decisions, and design docs.

Read the code, propose a design, and get agreement before building.

architecture

Architecture decisions, module boundaries, coupling, layering, and system structure.

Organize by what changes together. Boundaries expose contracts, not internal steps.

domain-modeling

Data shapes, invariants, state transitions, parsing, and effects.

Illegal states must be unrepresentable in the domain core.

contract-first

Approve contracts (APIs, schemas, formats, module boundaries) before implementation.

Get approval for a contract before writing code that depends on it.

Interfaces and docs

api

REST API contracts: endpoints, fields, evolution, status codes, errors, pagination, idempotency.

Write the OpenAPI spec first. Preserve shipped consumers. Pick status by failure.

ui-design

Frontend UI, layouts, components, responsive behavior, accessibility, WCAG, keyboard, and focus.

Start from the user task and hierarchy. Remove any element the task does not need. WCAG 2.2 AA is the floor.

documentation

READMEs, runbooks, API docs, module docs, and comments for existing code.

Document only what needs prose. Keep docs near the code, contract, or team that maintains them.

Backend and security

database

Schemas, migrations, indexes, transactions, query plans, and locking.

Protect production data first: prove rollout, locking, and recovery before change.

async-systems

Message contracts and schemas, queues, streams, concurrency, ordering, and backpressure.

Every async boundary names its contract, owner, lifetime, backpressure, and failure semantics.

error-handling

Error types, propagation, retries, user messages, and recovery.

Errors carry context. Never catch without handling or re-raising.

security

Auth, secrets, crypto, input validation, dependency risk, and trust boundaries.

Fail closed. Parse at the boundary. Authorize at the operation. No secrets or PII in logs.

Production

observability

Production logs, metrics, traces, health checks, alerts, SLOs, and performance measurement.

No user-reachable service path ships blind.

performance

Profiling, latency, throughput, allocation, caching, and hot paths.

Measure before optimizing. Measure again before keeping the change.

release

Release prep and release-artifact sync, on request or approval.

Breaking changes bump major. Agents prepare releases; humans mutate shared environments.

Repo and tools

commit

Staging reviewed work, commit splits, and messages.

Commit only the reviewed slice. Stage files by name.

git-workflow

Branches, history edits, conflicts, rebases, recovery, and force-push.

Never rewrite shared history or skip recovery.

issue-tracking

Initiatives, epics, and issues in GitHub, Jira, or another tracker: drafting, sizing, linking, and status.

Initiative > epic > issue. Every issue fits in one sprint and closes on evidence.

scaffolding

New projects, package setup, quality tooling, CI, and repo structure.

No feature code before the toolchain proves it can fail and pass.

official-source-check

Version-sensitive framework, library, SDK, or platform behavior, checked against official sources.

Model memory is a hint, not evidence, for version-sensitive behavior.
